props.title: The NeverEnding Story
props.initialSlug: A lonely boy's book becomes a magical reality quest

sections.content: The NeverEnding Story (1984) revolutionized fantasy filmmaking with its seamless blend of practical effects and profound metaphysical themes. Wolfgang Petersen crafted a masterwork that directly addressed childhood depression and escapism through literature, years before Pan's Labyrinth (2006) would explore similar territory. The film's practical effects, including the luck dragon Falkor and the ancient Morla, showcase the height of pre-CGI creature design, rivaling the groundbreaking work in The Dark Crystal (1982) and Labyrinth (1986).

sections.content: The film's meta-narrative structure, where young Bastian reads a book that becomes increasingly real, influenced countless works that followed. Inception (2010) and The Matrix (1999) would later explore similar themes of nested realities, but The NeverEnding Story did it first with a child's perspective. The Nothing, representing the loss of imagination and hope, remains one of cinema's most conceptually ambitious antagonists.

Wolfgang Petersen's direction brings a distinctly German expressionist influence to children's fantasy, evident in the striking design of the Ivory Tower and the Southern Oracle. This European artistic sensibility, combined with universal themes, created a unique aesthetic that influenced later films like MirrorMask (2005) and Bridge to Terabithia (2007). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Impact on Modern Fantasy

sections.content: The film's practical effects renaissance continues to influence contemporary filmmaking. Where the Wild Things Are (2009) directly referenced The NeverEnding Story's tactile creature design, while The Shape of Water (2017) borrowed from its emotive practical character work. The theme of childhood trauma and loss, embodied in Bastian's grief over his mother, created a template for emotional depth in children's fantasy that echoes through works like Coraline (2009) and A Monster Calls (2016).
